title: The Bias Blind Spot
text:
In 2002 Emily Pronin, Daniel Lin and Lee Ross, working at Stanford University, published a set of studies on a curious asymmetry: people see bias in others much more easily than in themselves.

In one study, students read short descriptions of well-known biases, such as the tendency to take credit for success while blaming failure on circumstances, or to favor one's own group. For each, they rated how much they themselves showed the bias and how much the average American did. For nearly every bias, they rated themselves as less affected than the average person.

In another study, students took a test of social intelligence and were told, at random, that they had done well or poorly. Those told they had done poorly tended to judge the test as less valid, a classic self-serving response. Yet when the researchers then described this tendency to them, the students said it probably applied to others more than it had to them.

The researchers argued that people judge their own bias by looking inward. They search their thoughts and feelings, find no sense of being biased, and conclude they are objective. Other people's bias, by contrast, is judged from their behavior, where it is visible. The pattern came to be called the bias blind spot.
lesson: Introspection cannot reveal your own biases, because they do not feel like anything from the inside. Ask others to check your reasoning, and use checklists or outside views where it matters.
people: Emily Pronin, Daniel Lin, Lee Ross
source: Pronin, E., Lin, D. Y., and Ross, L. (2002). The bias blind spot: Perceptions of bias in self versus others. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 28(3), 369-381.
